Brugmansia |genus = Brugmansia |species = suaveolens |authority = (Humb. & Bonpl. ex Willd.) [[Friedrich von Berchtold|Bercht.]] & [[Jan Svatopluk Presl|J.Presl]] |synonyms = ''Datura suaveolens''
''Datura gardneri'' Hook. }} '''''Brugmansia suaveolens''''', '''Brazil's white angel trumpet''', also known as '''angel's tears''' and '''snowy angel's trumpet''', is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the nightshade family [[Solanaceae]], native to south eastern Brazil, but thought to be extinct in the wild. Like several other species of ''Brugmansia'', it exists as an [[introduced species]] in areas outside its native range. It is a tender [[shrub]] or small [[tree]] with large semi-[[evergreen]] leaves and fragrant yellow or white trumpet-shaped flowers. ==Description== ''Brugmansia suaveolens'' is a semi-woody shrub or small tree, growing up to {{convert| 3|-|5|m|abbr=on|0}} tall, often with a many-branched trunk. The leaves are oval, to {{convert|25|cm|abbr=on|0}} long by {{convert|15|cm|abbr=on|0}} wide, and even larger when grown in the shade. The flowers, which tend to be white in colour, are sweetly scented at night and early morning, about {{convert|24|-|32|cm|abbr=on|0}} long and shaped like trumpets. The corolla body is slightly recurved to 5 main points, but the very peaks in the true species are always curved outwards, never rolled back, and these peaks are short, only {{convert|1|-|2.5|cm|abbr=on|1}} long. The flowers are usually white but may be yellow or pink and hang downward from fully pendulous up to nearly horizontal. ==Taxonomy== First discovered by [[Alexander von Humboldt]] and [[Aimé Bonpland]], ''Brugmansia suaveolens'' was first formally described and published by [[Carl Ludwig Willdenow]] in 1809 as ''Datura suaveolens''. In 1823, [[Friedrich von Berchtold]] and [[Jan Svatopluk Presl|Jan Presl]] transferred these to ''Brugmansia suaveolens''. Local common names include Maikoa, Huanduc, Maikiua, Tompeta del jucio, Tsuaak, Toe, Wahashupa, Peji, Bikut, Ohuetagi, Ain-vai, Baikua, Canachiari, and Ishauna.{{ cite book | author = Aronson, J. K. | title = Meyler's Side Effects of Herbal Medicines | edition = 15 | year = 2008 | page = 215 | publisher = Elsevier | isbn = 978-0-444-53269-5 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=ibxfK1l6oXoC&pg=PA215 }}{{ cite book | last = Nordegren | first = T. | title = The A-Z Encyclopedia of Alcohol and Drug Abuse | page = 409 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=4yaGePenGKgC&q=maikoa%20suaveolens&pg=PA409 | isbn = 978-1-58112-404-0 | year = 2002 | publisher = Universal-Publishers }} There are thousands of cultivated ''Brugmansia'' hybrids, and the majority have at least some ''B. suaveolens'' heritage.{{cite web | url = http://ibrugs.com/portals/0/ibrugs%20namelist.htm | title = Namelist of Established Cultivars | publisher = International Brugmansia & Datura Society | access-date = 2011-12-03 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20130326002411/http://ibrugs.com/portals/0/ibrugs%20namelist.htm | archive-date = 2013-03-26 | url-status = dead }} Some of the more popular cultivars include 'Dr. Seuss', 'Frosty Pink' and 'Charles Grimaldi'. ===Etymology=== The Latin [[binomial nomenclature|specific epithet]] ''suaveolens'' means "with a sweet fragrance".{{cite book |last=Harrison |first=Lorraine |title=RHS Latin for Gardeners |year=2012 |publisher=Mitchell Beazley |location=United Kingdom |isbn=978-1845337315 }} ==Distribution and habitat== ''B. suaveolens'' was originally [[endemism|endemic]] to the coastal rainforests of south-east Brazil, where it grows below {{convert|1000|m|ft|abbr=on}} along river banks and forest edges with warm temperatures, high humidity, and heavy rainfall. As a result of human interaction with this species, it can now be found growing in residential areas throughout much of South America; and occasionally in Central America, Mexico, California, Greece, Africa and even in parts of Florida.{{cite web| url = https://florida.plantatlas.usf.edu/Plant.aspx?id=294 | title = Atlas of Florida Vascular Plants |author1=Wunderlin, R. P. |author2=Hansen, B. F. | year = 2008 | publisher = Institute for Systematic Botany, University of South Florida, Tampa | access-date = 2011-12-04}} ==Ecology== Fragrant in the evenings to attract pollinating moths, they hang half-closed during the day, but return to their peak again in the evenings.{{ cite book | last = Barwick | first = M. | title = Tropical and Subtropical Trees: An Encyclopedia | publisher = Timber Press | year = 2004 | isbn = 978-0-88192-661-3 }} Brugmansia have two main stages to their life cycle. In the initial vegetative stage the young seedling grows straight up on usually a single stalk, until it reaches its first main fork at {{convert|80|–|150|cm|ft|abbr=on}} high. It will not flower until after it has reached this fork, and then only on new growth above the fork. Cuttings taken from lower vegetative region must also grow to a similar height before flowering, but cuttings from the upper flowering region will often flower at a very low height.
One interesting example of plant/animal interaction involves the butterfly ''Placidula euryanassa'', who uses ''Brugmansia suaveolens'' as one of its main larval foods. It has been shown that these can sequester the plant's tropane alkaloids and store them through the [[pupa]]l stage on to the adult butterfly, where they are then used as a defense mechanism, making themselves less palatable to [[vertebrate]] predators.{{ cite book | last = Eich | first = E. | title = Solanaceae and convolvulaceae - secondary metabolites | pages = 157, 158 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=ZpYtUED_DSsC&q=scopolamine+truth+drug+brugmansia&pg=PA157 | isbn = 978-3-540-74540-2 | date = 2008-01-12 | publisher = Springer }} [[File:Brugmansia 29.jpg|thumb|alt=''Brugmansia suaveolens''|Pink flowered ''Brugmansia suaveolens'']]The species is invasive in [[New Caledonia]].{{Cite book|url=https://horizon.documentation.ird.fr/exl-doc/pleins_textes/divers12-08/010052239.pdf|title=LES ESPÈCES EXOTIQUES ENVAHISSANTES DE NOUVELLE-CALÉDONIE|last=Hequet|first=Vanessa|year=2009|pages=17|language=fr}}[[File:Angel Trumpets shrub -- Brugmansia suaveolens.jpg|thumb|300px|''Brugmansia suaveolens'' on the Texas Gulf Coast]] [[File:Angel Trumpets -- Brugmansia suaveolens.jpg|thumb|200px|''Brugmansia suaveolens'']] ==Uses== Flower extracts of the plant have shown pain-killing ([[antinociceptive]]) activity in mice.{{ cite journal |author1=Parker, A. G. |author2=Peraza, G. G. |author3=Sena, J. |author4=Silva, E. S. |author5=Soares, M. C. |author6=Vaz, M. R. |author7=Furlong, E. B. |author8=Muccillo-Baisch, A. L. | title = Antinociceptive Effects of the Aqueous Extract of ''Brugmansia suaveolens'' Flowers in Mice | journal = Biological Research for Nursing | year = 2007 | volume = 8 | issue = 3 | pages = 234–239 | doi = 10.1177/1099800406293984 | pmid = 17172322 |s2cid=24325338 }} This antinociceptive activity may be related in part to [[benzodiazepine receptors]].{{ cite journal |author1=Muccillo-Baisch, A. L. |author2=Parker, A. G. |author3=Cardoso, G. P. |author4=Cezar-Vaz, M. R. |author5=Soares, M. C. | title = Evaluation of the Analgesic Effect of Aqueous Extract of ''Brugmansia suaveolens'' Flower in Mice: Possible Mechanism Involved | journal = Biological Research for Nursing | year = 2010 | volume = 11 | issue = 4 | pages = 345–350 | doi = 10.1177/1099800409354123 | pmid = 20338896 |s2cid=45521800 }}
''B. suaveolens'' is included in the [[Tasmania]]n Fire Service's list of low [[flammability]] plants, indicating that it is suitable for growing within a building protection zone.{{cite web|last1=Chladil and Sheridan|first1=Mark and Jennifer|title=Fire retardant garden plants for the urban fringe and rural areas|url=http://www.fire.tas.gov.au/publications/1709%20Brochure.pdf|website=www.fire.tas.gov.au|publisher=Tasmanian Fire Research Fund}} The flowers and the seeds are also traditionally used in [[Rio Grande do Sul]], southern Brazil, mixed in water and ingested for its [[analgesic]]-like effect.
Many South American cultures have been noted to use ''Brugmansia suaveolens'' [[ritually]]. The Ingano and Siona in the Putumayo region both use it as an [[entheogen]]. It is also used by some Amazonian tribes as an admixture to increase the potency of [[Ayahuasca]].{{cite book | last = Pratt | first = C. | title = An Encyclopedia of Shamanism | volume = 1 | pages = 68, 69 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=HltJMMq1_60C&q=brugmansia%20suaveolens&pg=PA68 | isbn = 978-1-4042-1040-0 | date = 2007-08-01 | publisher = The Rosen Publishing Group }} In some South American countries, it is known to be occasionally added to ayahuasca brews by [[malevolent sorcerer]]s or bad shamans who wish to take advantage of unsuspecting tourists. Genuine shamans believe one of the purposes for this is to "steal one's energy and/or power", of which they believe every person has a limited stockpile.Campos, Don Jose (2011). The Shaman & Ayahuasca: Journeys to Sacred Realms. ==Cultivation== ''Brugmansia'' are grown as ornamentals outdoors year-round in non-freezing climates around the world. They do not tolerate temperatures that fall significantly below {{convert|5|C|F}} Like other large-leaved, fast-growing plants, they appreciate a little protection from the wind, as well as from the hottest afternoon sun. They like organically rich soil, frequent water, and heavy fertilizer when in full growth. Both woody and leafy tip cuttings are used to propagate ''Brugmansia'', although thicker cuttings tolerate lower humidity. In northern climes they are often grown out in large containers and wintered over in non-freezing garages or basements.{{cite book |author1=Preissel, U. |author2=Preissel, H.-G. | title = Brugmansia and Datura: Angel's Trumpets and Thorn Apples | publisher = Firefly Books | year = 2002 | location = Buffalo, New York | pages = 106–129 | isbn = 978-1-55209-598-0 }} Alternatively they are suitable for a sunny conservatory. They may be trained as standards (with a single, straight trunk). In cultivation in the [[United Kingdom|UK]] this plant has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].{{cite web | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/79128/i-Brugmansia-suaveolens-i/Details | title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Brugmansia suavolens'' | access-date=12 January 2018}} ==Toxicity== {{Further|Brugmansia#Toxicity}} Every part of ''Brugmansia suaveolens'' is poisonous, with the seeds and leaves being especially dangerous.{{ cite book | title = Biology Digest | publisher = Plexus Publications | year = 1991 | volume = 18 | page = 23 | lccn = 75646463 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=xB5ZAAAAYAAJ&q=brugmansia }} As in other species of ''Brugmansia'', ''B. suaveolens'' is rich in [[scopolamine]] (hyoscine), [[hyoscyamine]], [[atropine]], and several other [[tropane alkaloids]].{{cite journal |author1=Evans, W. C. |author2=Lampard, J. F. | year = 1972 | title = Alkaloids of ''Datura suaveolens'' | journal = Phytochemistry | volume = 11 | issue = 11 | pages = 3293–3298 | doi = 10.1016/S0031-9422(00)86392-X |bibcode=1972PChem..11.3293E }} Effects of ingestion can include paralysis of [[Smooth muscle tissue|smooth muscles]], confusion, delusions, [[tachycardia]], dry mouth, constipation, visual and auditory hallucinations, [[mydriasis]], rapid onset [[cycloplegia]], and death.{{ cite journal |author1=van der Donck, I. |author2=Mulliez, E. |author3=Blanckaert, J. | title = Angel's Trumpet (''Brugmansia arborea'') and mydriasis in a child - A case report | journal = Bulletin de la Société Belge d'Ophtalmologie | year = 2004 | volume = 292 |issue=292 | pages = 53–56 | pmid = 15253491 | url = https://www.ophthalmologia.be/download.php?dof_id=223 }}{{ cite book | author = Wagstaff, D. J. | title = International poisonous plants checklist: an evidence-based reference | publisher = CRC Press | year = 2008 | page = 69 | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=h7tbd-5ZAQ8C&q=datura%20%20suaveolens%20fatal&pg=PA69 | isbn = 978-1-4200-6252-6 }}{{ cite book | author = Greenburg, M. I. | title = Disaster! - A Compendium of Terrorist, Natural and Man-Made Catastrophes | year = 2006 | page = 84 | publisher = Jones & Bartlett Learning | url = https://books.google.com/books?id=EZAdQAuPyKAC&q=datura%20%20suaveolens%20death&pg=PA84 | isbn = 978-0-7637-3989-8 }} ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== {{Commonscat}} *[http://www.mobot.org/GARDENINGHELP/PLANTFINDER/Plant.asp?Code=A491 Kemper Center] *[https://mygrandpasocks.org Botany Photo of the Day] {{Taxonbar|from=Q3314772}} [[Category:Brugmansia|suaveolens]] [[Category:Taxa named by Aimé Bonpland]] [[Category:Taxa named by Alexander von Humboldt]]
